paragraphs.text: "I deserve a treat after all that shopping," Cecil said, pausing in front of a smoothie store.
Mia laughed. "Buying new shoes isn't that hard."
Suddenly they heard a commotion behind them, and a female voice yelled, "Help!"
Cecil and Mia turned around and saw a man lying on the ground.
"My husband collapsed!" the woman cried.
"I'll dial 9-1-1," Cecil said, pulling out his phone.
The woman dropped to her knees beside her husband. "He's not breathing!"
People gathered around, looking worried, but no one moved to help.
"This is 9-1-1," the operator said. "What is your emergency?"
Cecil told the operator his name and location and explained the situation before passing his phone to the woman.
"I'm Stephanie Hart," she said. She answered a few questions, then her eyes went wide. "I don't know how to do CPR, but I'll try!"

Cecil put his phone on speaker mode so Mrs. Hart could hear the operator's instructions. Mrs. Hart put her hands on her husband's chest and began to press. Soon an ambulance arrived and paramedics jumped out. One of them quickly checked Mr. Hart before taking over CPR from Mrs. Hart. Within seconds the man was breathing, and the paramedics put him in the ambulance.
"That was awful," Mia said.
Cecil nodded.
That evening Cecil recounted the frightening episode to his family.
"You did the right thing by calling 9-1-1," Dad said.
"I wanted to do more," Cecil said.
"I've seen two-hour CPR courses with certified instructors at the community college," Dad said.
Cecil smiled. "Let's sign up!"
Two weeks later Cecil and Dad attended the class.

Miss Reese, the instructor, stood behind a desk in front of the room. A training dummy of a man's head and torso was propped against the desk. "CPR saves lives," she began. "When the heart stops due to something like a heart attack or near drowning, blood circulation stops too. It only takes minutes for brain damage to occur. CPR keeps blood flowing to the brain to help prevent damage. We'll start by learning how to perform CPR on an adult. Does anyone know what to do first?"
Cecil half-raised his hand, and Miss Reese called on him. "Call 9-1-1?" he said hesitantly.
"That's right!" the instructor said. "Why don't you come up and help me demonstrate?"
Dad gave Cecil an encouraging smile, and Cecil made his way to the front of the classroom.
Miss Reese placed the dummy on the floor. "First check whether Darrell the Dummy is conscious."
Cecil knelt beside the dummy. "Umm, Darrell? Can you hear me?"
"Darrell's not responsive," Miss Reese said.
"He's definitely unconscious," Cecil agreed.
"Next," Miss Reese said, "check if Darrell is breathing." She showed Cecil how to put his ear near Darrell's mouth and nose to listen for breathing.
"He's not breathing," Cecil said.

"Since Darrell is unconscious and not breathing, that means we should perform CPR," Miss Reese said. "He needs to be on his back on a firm surface, and luckily he already is. Before starting CPR though, we need to make sure his airway is clear. We can't perform CPR if Darrell's airway is obstructed. Tilt the head back and lift the chin. Then check inside Darrell's mouth for anything that might cause him to choke."
Cecil did as Miss Reese told him. "It’s clear."
"Now we can start chest compressions," Miss Reese said.
Following Miss Reese's instructions, Cecil put a hand in the center of the dummy's chest. He placed his other hand on top of the first. With his elbows stiff, he pushed down on the dummy's chest.

"A little harder," Miss Reese said. "Push five to six centimeters—about a third of the depth of the chest. Keep going at about 100 to 120 compressions per minute until the person begins breathing or help arrives."
Cecil pushed and pushed—it was hard work!
"He's breathing!" Miss Reese announced to applause from the class.
Dad and the other members of the class took turns saving Darrell. Cecil even tried another rescue himself, feeling more confident the second time.
After class Cecil and Dad met Mia at the smoothie store and told her about what they had learned.
"It's scary to think that any one of these people could collapse," Mia said, looking out the store windows.
"It's very unlikely," Dad said.
"I hope I never have to use CPR, but I feel better now that I know what to do," Cecil said. "Maybe you could take the class too."
Mia smiled. "I'm going to sign up!"
"Ha-ha!" Martin laughed as Laura looked for the breakfast cereal. "The Frosted Loops are all gone—I ate them all!"
Laura scowled at her little brother, grabbed a banana, and sat down. Her older sister was dressed in her taekwondo uniform, bragging about her lessons.
"My test is tomorrow, and I'm definitely going to get a black belt because I'm the best . . . " Willow's voice went on.
"Morning, Mom," Laura said as her mother hurried past carrying books. Mom's latest charity project was collecting books for a homeless shelter. She was so busy with that, she didn't notice Laura.

"Being the middle child stinks," Laura thought suddenly. Willow got lots of attention for taekwondo. Martin got even more attention because he was constantly getting into trouble. Laura sometimes felt lost among her family—invisible even.
Mom finally noticed her. "Oh, Laura, I have a task for you."
"I have lots of homework," Laura protested. "I also want to do some baking."
"Baking again?" Mom smiled. "You're just like Great-Grandmother Lucy!"
Laura had heard stories about Lucy, who had been a middle child too. Just like Laura, she had loved to bake. She had even created her own recipes.
"This won't take long," Mom said. "Go through your old belongings in the attic and gather some books for my donation pile."
Laura flicked on the attic light and quickly spotted the storage bin with her old books. She grabbed a few books and dropped them into a bag. "Done!" she thought. "Now it's baking time!"
Just then a dusty box labeled Lucy's Cookbooks caught her eye. Intrigued, Laura knelt down and lifted the flaps. Dust flew into the air, oddly swirling above an old scrapbook.
" Baking Magic ," Laura read. "Cool—Lucy's recipes!" On page one there was a strange inscription: " Recipes for a sweet family. Magic lasts for three hours ."
Minutes later Laura stood in the kitchen, trying to decide which recipe to try while Martin read over her shoulder.
"Ooh," he said, "'Sticky Sweet Honey Buns.' Bake those!"
Laura shrugged. "Okay."
Soon the smell of honey filled the kitchen. Laura handed Martin a warm bun. He quickly ate it. She waited for his insults, but instead he suddenly threw his arms around her.
"I'll never tease you again," Martin said. "I love you!"
"Huh?" Laura hugged him back, her eyes landing on Baking Magic . Martin had never acted this sweetly—did Lucy's recipe have anything to do with it?
A while later Willow and Mom tried the buns too.
"Delicious!" Willow said. "Fantastic! I wish I was good at baking like you!"

"Your great-grandma's recipes always tasted so . . . magical," Mom said with a smile. She sat down at the kitchen table and patted the chair next to her. "Come sit down, Laura. It's been so long since we've had a nice talk."

For an hour everyone praised Laura, giving her lots of attention, as they ate the rest of the honey buns. Finally Laura headed to the computer to start working on her stack of homework assignments. She grinned, remembering the inscription in the cookbook. Lucy's magical recipes had definitely worked!
As Laura typed, Martin leaned in from behind her. "Need any help?"
"Thanks, but—"
He leaned closer. "I'll just keep you company then."
"Laura!" Mom called from upstairs. "I miss you!"
"You just saw me," Laura mumbled.
Willow poked her head in the room. "Are you going to do more baking? You're the best baker—no, you're the best sister ever!"
"I'm your only sister," Laura thought. As she typed, she couldn't concentrate because Martin kept complimenting her.
Then Mom entered the room. "Let's go shopping, Laura! I want to spend the rest of the day with you."
Willow tugged at Laura's arm. "Teach me how to bake just like you do!"
Laura buried her face in her hands, telling herself that the magic would wear off soon. She couldn't wait to return to being the family's invisible middle child.
In the meantime she had one more task to complete: adding Baking Magic to Mom's donation pile!
Caroline pedaled up the driveway, looking for a spot to park her bike. Her usual spot was occupied by junk Dad had found at a flea market—tools, flower pots, and an old yellow surfboard.
"Caroline!" Dad ran outside, sounding worried. "You're late again . . . why didn't you text me?"
Caroline sighed. "Relax, Dad, I was just talking to kids from jazz band."
"Oh! Do they live in Luna Bay, and are they. . . ?"
"Ugh, here we go again!" Caroline thought, annoyed. Ever since she'd started middle school, Dad had been questioning her about every aspect of her life. He asked about her friends, her plans, her—
"Hey!" Dad's face lit up. "Let's invite your friends to eat tacos with us on Tuesday! Do they like tacos?"
"No!" Caroline said. "I mean, maybe they like tacos, but I'm not inviting Austin and Betsy over."
"Why not?"
"Because you'll interrogate them!"
"I promise," he started, placing a hand over his heart, "no questions! I won't even ask them to pass the hot sauce!"
"Then you'll find another way to humiliate me . . . like singing really old songs! So no, absolutely not!"
"Okay," Dad mumbled with hurt in his voice.
The following week Caroline stayed after school every day for jazz band, remembering to text Dad. But on Wednesday, when she biked home with Austin, she forgot.
Dad was annoyed but let it go. On Friday, after rehearsal ran late, Caroline pulled out her phone and panicked. Her battery was dead!
She looked around, hoping to borrow a phone from her friends, but Betsy and Austin had already left. Finally she hopped on her bike and breathlessly pedaled home, where she explained what happened.
"That's not an excuse!" Dad snapped. "You've been late multiple times without informing me, so from now on, I'm picking you up from rehearsal."
"That's totally ridiculous—I'm not in kindergarten!" Caroline persisted and kept arguing, but Dad wouldn't budge.
On Saturday Dad gave Caroline permission to go to Betsy's house before he mysteriously left. After last night's argument, she was still feeling angry at him.
Austin was already at Betsy's house when she arrived. "Let's go down to Luna Beach," he said.

A few minutes later, they reached the ocean. The blue water glistened in the sunlight, and tall waves curled toward the shore. Surfers in wet suits were out in the water, struggling to stand on their boards while an instructor bellowed tips.
"Whoa!" Austin said as a huge wave tossed a man off his board. "That dude had a spectacular wipeout!"
Caroline watched the surfer climb back on his yellow board. As he started paddling, she gasped. "That's my father!"
Betsy laughed. "Your dad takes surfing lessons?"
"Apparently!" Caroline stiffened, waiting for her friends to poke fun at her dad, but instead they sounded impressed.
"Awesome," Austin said.
"He's got guts!" Betsy said.
Caroline shook her head, still unable to comprehend what she was seeing. "Do you guys mind if we get out of here?"
That night at dinner, the air still felt tense. Caroline stayed quiet as Dad passed the potatoes.
"How was your afternoon?"
Caroline pushed some peas around. "Betsy lives near the ocean, so we walked to Luna Beach, and . . ." She glanced up, inhaling sharply before blurting out, "We watched some surfers and I saw you!"
Dad nearly dropped his fork.
"Why didn't you tell me about the surfing lessons?"
He hung his head. "It sounds dumb, but I was too embarrassed. I wanted to feel confident that I could actually surf first." He sighed. "I didn't want to talk about it until I was ready."
Caroline nodded slowly. "I get it because sometimes I don't feel like talking about stuff either. But you keep asking—"

"Too many questions," Dad jumped in. "I've been thinking . . . You can ride your bike home from rehearsal. And from now on, I'll try to give you some space when you don't feel like talking." He cast a hopeful look at her. "It might help if I could meet your new friends."
"Well, guess what—they want to meet you too."
"Huh?" This time Dad did drop his fork.
Caroline grinned. "They think it's cool you're a surfer, so I invited them over for dinner on Tuesday!"

Hayley rolled on her skateboard to the top of the concrete ramp, carefully shifting her weight as she came to a stop. "I did it!" she thought triumphantly, before losing her balance and tumbling backward.
A group of nearby skateboarders laughed.
"Not even close to one of Logan's tricks," one teased.
"Where is Logan?" Hayley suddenly wondered. The two of them met at the skate park every Saturday—and he'd promised to help her perfect this trick today.
She checked her phone, but his last text was from three days earlier. They'd made plans to meet at the library, but he hadn't shown up. Instead a text had arrived after midnight: "Sorry. I forgot."
"Where are you?" she typed now. "Is everything okay?"

On Monday in Spanish class, Señora Ramos handed back the students' graded tests. Hayley felt relieved to see Logan in his seat since she hadn't heard a word from him over the weekend. But she also felt irritated that he'd been ditching her so frequently, and today he hadn't even acknowledged her by waving or anything.
She was about to try to catch his eye when she spotted the test on his desk. The grade was shocking.
"Logan got a D?" Hayley thought. "What in the world is going on with him lately?"
As the days passed, Hayley rarely saw Logan. "Is he avoiding me?" she wondered. Had she done something to offend him?
She kept checking his online profile, and everything seemed normal. Then one day she spotted him sitting alone outside at a table near the guidance counselors' offices.
"Hey, Logan," she called, "are you okay? You haven't been—"
"I'm fine," Logan snapped.

Provoked by his tone, Hayley heard herself snapping back. "There's no need to be so grouchy—I was only asking how you're doing! I guess you don't care that you're throwing away our friendship with your constant disappearing act. But if that's what you want, then—"
"Ugh!" Logan got up and stormed off in a huff, leaving Hayley confused, angry, and utterly hurt.
"Is something wrong, Hayley?"
She looked up to see Mr. Obi, one of the guidance counselors.
"No, I'm fine, but thanks for asking."
"You don't look fine. But I'm here to listen if you feel like talking," Mr. Obi said.
As much as Hayley didn't want to talk, she suddenly found herself blurting out all her confusion and frustration with Logan. She was careful, though, to avoid mentioning his name.
Mr. Obi listened quietly until she was finished. "From what you've told me, it sounds like your friend may be depressed."
A wave of guilt washed over Hayley. "I didn't think of that."

"Depression is a common condition—in fact, one in five teens experiences it," Mr. Obi explained. "People with depression often feel hopeless and irritable. Their sleep patterns and appetites can change. They can also have trouble concentrating and may even lose interest in favorite activities. Sometimes that means they isolate themselves from friends."
"Is there anything I can do for Lo—I mean my friend . . . if he's depressed?" Hayley asked.

Mr. Obi nodded with a sympathetic smile. "You can let him know that you care, and you're available to listen. Try to stay in touch so your friend doesn't feel alone. If he won't talk to you, encourage him to talk to someone else. And if you ever think he's in serious trouble, you should let an adult know immediately."

"Thanks, Mr. Obi—that information is helpful." Wondering how much time was left before her next class, Hayley checked her phone. On the screen was a new notification: Logan had posted something on his online profile.
Hayley's hands began to tremble as she showed the counselor her phone. "Mr. Obi, I think Logan needs help."
"Yes!" Hayley cheered. She had just executed the new trick perfectly. Even the skateboarders who usually teased her were impressed, giving her a round of applause.
"Great job!" someone said.
"You're here!" Hayley rolled down the ramp to greet Logan. "I wasn't sure if you saw my text."

Logan nodded. "Thanks for staying in touch with me over the last few months. Mr. Obi reached out too—and recommended that I see a therapist. I'm feeling better now, except . . . " He looked away for a second. "Sorry I was a jerk to you."
"No need to apologize!" Hayley said quickly. "Do you want to talk about anything?"
Logan shook his head. "Not really—some stuff just happened at home with my parents."
"Understood. I'm here to listen if you need it."
"Thanks. But for now, how about we just skate?" he said before hopping on his board to perform a kick flip.
For the first time in weeks, Hayley saw her friend smile.
Dinner was over, but Quinn was still sitting at the kitchen table, talking to Mom and Grandpa.
"What was the most boring thing that happened at school today?" Grandpa asked teasingly.

Quinn was eager to complain about math class. "My teacher gave us the most boring assignment ever—Statistics and You. "We have to use two different kinds of graphs to illustrate statistics that affect our lives. I don't know any statistics, never mind some that affect me. Where do I start?"
"You could start right here," Grandpa suggested. "Why am I having dinner with you?"
"Because you're staying with us temporarily after falling and breaking your wrist."
Grandpa nodded. "Now take out your phone and look up some statistics on older Americans and falls."

Quinn quickly found an article online and read part of it aloud. "'Every year one in four Americans aged 65 and over falls. These 29 million falls lead to 27 thousand deaths.' That's a lot of falls, but how do these statistics affect me? I'm not over 65."
"Where are you sleeping tonight?" Grandpa asked.

"On the living room couch because you're sleeping in my bed . . . Oh, I get it! You're one of those older Americans who fell. The statistics are about seniors, but their problems affect their families too."
"Exactly." Grandpa turned to Mom. "When my wrist heals, I should take a class at your fitness center to improve my balance."
"That's a great idea," she said, "if we're still open. People used to exercise when they got off work at the candy factory. But business has declined since the factory shut down two months ago."
Quinn realized that her life would definitely be affected if Mom's fitness center went out of business. "Hey, Mom, do you keep track of how many clients work out every day?"
"Yes," Mom said.
"I just got an idea for my math project, but I need to know how many people have used the center in the past six months."
A few nights later, Quinn delivered a presentation at the kitchen table.

"This is a single-line graph," she announced, holding up a paper. "It shows the number of people who have used the fitness center in the past six months. The figures are fairly constant for the first four months. But once the factory closes, they drop by 23 percent."
Mom looked worried. "And I know new memberships are down too!"

"But there's also some promising news," Quinn said. "The number of older Americans is growing. That's partly due to improved medical care, which has boosted life expectancy. Only 42 percent of babies born in 1900 could expect to live past 65. But for people born in 2000, that number is projected to almost double."
"So there are more old people now," Grandpa said. "How is that good news?"

"Compare these two pie charts," Quinn said. "The U.S. Census Bureau collects and compiles lots of statistics, so I looked up some census data for our town. Like the rest of the U.S., people over 65 made up around 12 percent of the population in 2000. But now that number has increased to 15 percent, and it's expected to grow even more."
"Maybe I should refocus my business for older members," Mom said. "Besides working on balance, I could offer strength-training, stretching, and aerobic exercises."
"You could conduct a survey to see if people are interested!" Quinn suggested.

"Oh, seniors are definitely interested," Grandpa said. "My friend Jim says his walking group can't meet during winter because the park's paths get icy. So his group would love senior fitness classes too."
"That's what my math teacher calls anecdotal evidence, Grandpa," Quinn said. "You're drawing conclusions based only on your opinion—and Jim's."
Grandpa pretended to be angry. "I've known Jim since high school! We're really smart guys!"

Quinn laughed. "Yes, but you two are from the same segment of the population. You're the exact same age, and you're both men. It would be better to hear from a wider demographic through a random survey including people of different ages and genders. This would give Mom a more representative sample of the senior community."
"I could draw up the questions," Mom said, "but how will we obtain a representative sample?"

"That's easy," Grandpa said. "Everyone eats at the Supreme Diner on Tuesdays because it's Senior Discount Day. The diner's next door to your fitness center, so I could survey people passing by. Plus there are seniors of all ages and genders—that's a wider demographic."
Quinn nodded. "After you've gathered the data, I could help Mom interpret it. And if my teacher gives me extra credit for that, statistics could have a positive effect on my math grade!"
Jacob sat with the Christmas present from his grandparents on his lap while the whole family looked on.

"Let me guess," he said, slowly unwrapping the box with a forced smile. "Socks again?" He opened the box and found a piece of paper instead. It was a handwritten note that read: "Merry Christmas! You, Jacob Price, are the owner of five shares of Orange Software Company's stock."
"Instead of socks, we got you stock!" Grandpa said.
"Thank you, Grandpa and Grandma!" Jacob said. "I love Orange's games! Does this mean I'm going to be rich?"
Everyone laughed.

"Come with me," Grandpa said. He led Jacob into his office as the rest of the family opened their last presents. "Your grandmother and I wanted to give you something different this year. Your parents told us not to give you money since you'd just spend it."
Jacob grinned sheepishly. "What else can you do with money besides save or spend it?"
"You can invest it," Grandpa said. "Your present this year is an introduction to investing in the stock market."
Jacob looked down at the note again. "I'm an owner—but I don't own the whole company, right?"
Grandpa smiled. "Right. You own stock in the company. Stock is ownership in the company. You own five shares. A share is a unit of ownership. Companies sell stock to raise money."
"Don't they make enough money with their products?" Jacob asked. "Orange Software has a new game coming out soon—it's going to sell millions of copies!"

"Orange makes a lot of money, but companies always need more money to help them expand or compete with other companies. They can use the money from selling stock to develop new products or improve existing ones. They can also use the money to hire employees or cover other business costs."
Jacob nodded. "Now I get why companies sell stock. But how do people make money buying it?"

"It's an investment—using money to make more money," Grandpa said. "If a company does well, and its profits go up, stock owners share in the profits. Then they can sell their stock at a higher price than they first paid."
"Cool," Jacob said. "Money that grows!"
"It can also go the other way," Grandpa warned. "Investing is often risky. If the company loses money, the stock price goes down. There's no guarantee which way it will go."
Jacob didn't think much about his present until one morning a few weeks later.
"Orange's latest game has already sold thousands of copies since its release," Dad said from behind a newspaper. "The stock price increased 7 percent."
"Does that mean I'm making money?"
"Yep." Dad showed Jacob the stock market section of the paper, pointing to Orange Software's listing.
"Whoa!" Jacob said. "I made $17.50!"

Soon Jacob began paying more attention to the stock market, checking Orange Software's stock every day. Some days it increased a little, while other days it increased a lot. Then there were days when the stock price dropped a little. And one day, after a serious glitch was discovered in a game, the price dropped a lot.
When Grandpa called, Jacob talked to him about it.

"Don't worry too much about little ups or downs," Grandpa said. "It's better to think in the long term with investing. Stock prices go up and down every day. Focus on whether a stock does well or not over a longer period of time."
For the next year, Jacob tracked Orange's stock. By the following Christmas, it had doubled in price. Jacob had also been working on saving a lot of his allowance.
"I'm thinking about buying more stock someday," he said to Grandpa.

"I did lots of research before buying stock in Orange," Grandpa said. "Big or popular companies aren't always a wise choice. It's important to read about a company in order to make a smart investment."
"Got it," Jacob said.
After dinner, when it was time to open presents, Jacob reached for Grandpa and Grandma's package first.
"More stock?" he asked, eagerly tearing into the present.
"Since you've already learned about the stock market and investing . . . " Grandpa grinned. "We went back to—"
Jacob laughed. "Socks!"

7.title: Look Up from Your Cell Phone!

paragraphs.text: Peter was enjoying breakfast in his favorite spot, in front of the kitchen window.
"It's 7:15," Grandma said. "Shouldn't you leave for school?" She was staying with Peter while his parents were away.
"I can leave at 7:25 and not be late!" Peter said. "It's the best thing about living across the street from school."

Just then they heard the screech of tires outside. Grandma looked out the window and saw a car stopped in the middle of the intersection. The driver leaned out the window to scold a girl from Peter's class.
Peter could easily guess what the driver was saying. He imitated him aloud: "Look where you're going, not at your phone!"
"He's right," Grandma said. "You have to look up when crossing the street."
"I know," Peter said. "But kids get distracted by their phones."
Grandma frowned. "Something should be done before someone gets hurt."
That day in art class, the teacher asked the students to create a public-service ad. "Make a sign that helps solve a problem in our community," she instructed.
Peter thought back to the incident at the intersection that morning. "I don't know if it will help," he thought, "but I have an idea."

He painted the words "Look Up!" in bright colors on a large board. Then he drew two pictures on the sign. One picture showed a person staring at a cell phone while crossing the street. Nearby a car was slamming on its brakes. Peter painted a red line through the picture.
The other picture was another person crossing the street. This person's eyes were focused ahead. A car patiently waited at the light.
"Great sign, Peter," the teacher said. "What inspired it?"
Peter explained the problem at the intersection.
"I almost got hit crossing there yesterday!" a girl exclaimed.
"Were you looking at your phone?" the teacher asked.
"I was watching a funny video." The girl shrugged. "I didn't want to miss the ending."
"Drivers should watch out for us," another student said.
"True," the teacher said. "But pedestrians also need to watch out for oncoming traffic. Nice work, Peter."
The teacher gave Peter his sign to take home and an A for the assignment.
After school Peter set his sign up so anyone crossing the intersection would see it. But moments later, Principal Axworth came and removed the sign.
"Who put this here and why?" he growled.
Peter gulped. He was too intimidated to reply, but he wasn't ready to give up. He knew he was going to need a strong argument to convince the principal to keep the sign.

Every morning for the rest of the week, Peter counted the number of honks and near-miss collisions. He calculated the average number of kids crossing the street and how many were looking at their phones. He also researched real-world statistics on traffic accidents. Finally he put his findings into a colorful chart comparing all his data. Now all he had to do was summon the courage to talk to Principal Axworth!

Peter went to school early Monday morning to see Principal Axworth. Peter explained the problem at the intersection. Using his chart, he showed the average daily number of kids crossing the street. He shared his data on how many kids were looking at their phones. Then he presented the number of car honks and near misses.

"Studies show that while traffic accidents are decreasing, cell phone-related pedestrian accidents are increasing," Peter explained. "People get so distracted by their phones, they become unaware of their surroundings. I thought a bright sign would remind students to look up."
"You've prepared a persuasive argument," the principal said. "We'll put your sign back up. And I'm going to suggest other schools in the city start a similar program."
Peter beamed. His sign really was going to help solve a community problem!

Ian stood at the window. Right outside a noisy robin fluttered about, but Ian scarcely noticed it. His eyes were focused instead on the backyard garden. Normally by Father's Day, strawberries that Dad had planted were ripening, and green beans were coiling up their poles. But this year the garden was just an ugly patch of dirt and weeds. Ian and Mom hadn't planted a thing.
Ian closed his eyes, remembering last year's Father's Day celebration. They'd gone to a baseball game, and later Dad had grilled hamburgers.
"Today is definitely going to be different," Ian thought glumly. It was the first Father's Day since Dad had died. And—
"Ian! Breakfast!" Mom called.
Downstairs, Ian poured syrup on his pancakes. "Are we doing anything today?" he asked blankly.

Mom looked up from her plate, quickly brushing away a few tears. "Yes," she said briskly. "We're going to Meadow Bird Sanctuary. It's a beautiful day, and there's a nice trail around the pond. We'll see lots of birds." She paused. "Dad loved watching birds."
Ian sighed. "I remember."
"What's a sanctuary anyway?" Ian asked as Mom parked in a gravel lot.
"I guess you could call it a place of refuge," Mom said. "It's land preserved for plants and wildlife, to keep them safe and help them thrive."
Ian saw some dense woods with trails forking off in different directions. A few people stood near a Welcome sign—a mother and a little girl and an older man with binoculars.
"Looks like a tour's about to start," Mom said. "Good."

A guide introduced herself as Beth, and the group set off. As they wandered through the woods, Beth pointed out various plants and trees. Ian couldn't keep track of any of the plants' names—except for the poison ivy creeping along the trail.
Suddenly Beth halted and pointed upward. "Look."
Ian gazed up at the branches of a tall tree. He saw a brown bird near a nest.
"A mommy bird!" the little girl cried. "She's feeding her babies!"
"Actually, that's a daddy bird," Beth said. "And since today is Father's Day, it's the perfect time to tell you that many birds make great fathers!"
The man with the binoculars nodded eagerly. "Birds actually make much better fathers than mammals do."

"That's true, Mr. Avery," Beth said. "While male mammals rarely feed their young, some male birds bring food to their babies. Plus, village weavers build nests, and emperor penguins keep eggs warm. Did you know that some male songbirds teach their sons how to sing?"
"Yes!" Mr. Avery burst out. "The white-throated sparrow does that!"
Ian and Mom exchanged grins. Mr. Avery was certainly very enthusiastic about birds. "Dad would love this guy!" Ian thought.

As they circled the pond, Beth showed them some wading birds. Ian stopped to watch a great blue heron. The tall bird stood silently in shallow water, waiting for fish to swim by. Its legs were so skinny and long, they made Ian think of brittle sticks.
Mr. Avery was watching too. "Bird-watching requires stillness and patience," he said quietly. "But it always brings me delight—and peace."
After the tour Ian and Mom bought some lunch and sat outside on a bench. The sun felt warm, and the air inside the sanctuary rang with birds' clear voices.
"This is Dad's kind of place," Ian said.
Mom smiled. "It sure is."
"I know what we should do when we get home," Ian said enthusiastically.
Mom looked at him. "What?"
"Plant some vegetables! Dad would have liked that too."
Cleo trudged into the kitchen after school.
"What's wrong?" Mom asked.
"Everyone is playing BattleQuest . It's a new online game, and it's the only thing Rea and Noah ever talk about." Cleo sighed. "I'm tired of being left out of the fun."
"Well, once you save enough allowance, you can join the fun," Mom said.
Cleo sighed. She went into the living room and plopped in front of the family computer. If she couldn't play BattleQuest herself, she'd have to settle for watching other people play.
She'd just finished watching a video when an ad flashed on the screen. Cleo couldn't believe her luck! "Free One-Day Trial of BattleQuest !" she read.

She clicked the link and entered a username, her email, and her favorite password. As the game downloaded, she had a sudden thought. "I should've asked Mom's permission. But it is free. It'll be fine."

When Cleo entered the world of BattleQuest , it somehow looked different from the videos. "This must be the latest version," she reasoned. She tried searching for her friends' IDs but couldn't find them. It didn't really matter though—Cleo was finally playing BattleQuest !
The next morning Cleo met Rea and Noah in the corridor at school. " BattleQuest is so much fun!" she exclaimed. "You didn't tell me there were dragons in the game!"
Rea and Noah looked at each other.
"Dragons?" Noah asked.
"I wish my free trial lasted longer than one day." Cleo sighed.
"What are you talking about . . . ?" Rea began when Cleo's phone chirped.
Cleo checked her phone and saw a text from her cousin. Just got a weird email from you. Spam ?
"That's strange," Cleo said when her phone chirped again. A friend from camp texted to say she got a similar email. Moments later Cleo's tennis coach also texted about spam.
"It sounds like you got hacked," Noah said.
Cleo wasn't looking forward to telling Mom about the spam emails, but it turned out she didn't have to. When she got home, Mom and Uncle Roger were hunched over the family computer.

"Then the screen went black," Mom explained. "A window popped up saying if I wanted my data, I'd have to pay a ransom. I couldn't—even if I wanted to! The bank put a hold on my account today after several suspicious charges."
"You got infected by ransomware. Good thing there's a security specialist in the family." Uncle Roger smiled. "Have either of you downloaded anything recently?"
"I haven't," Mom said. "Cleo?"
Cleo's cheeks turned red. "Does a free trial of BattleQuest count?"

"Absolutely," Uncle Roger said. "Hackers use links like that to trick people into installing malware on their computers. Then they take control of your computer and steal your personal information like passwords and banking information."
Cleo looked at Mom. "Sorry. BattleQuest is the only thing my friends talk about, and I was tired of feeling left out."

"I'm glad you told us," Uncle Roger said. "It will make it easier to fix the problem. Anyone can be a victim of identity theft, but there are steps people can take to be safer. To start, I'll install antivirus software to keep you safe from viruses and ransomware. I'll also set up a firewall."
"What's a firewall?" Cleo asked.

"It's a program that filters information coming from the internet into your computer," Uncle Roger explained. "It's like a window screen that keeps bugs out. But in order for a firewall to work, you have to scan your computer on a regular basis."
"Is there anything else we should do differently?" Mom asked, giving Cleo a stern look.
"Never reuse passwords," Uncle Roger said. "Watch out for links with misspellings and ads or pop-ups promising something for nothing."
"I've learned that the hard way," Cleo said. "'Free' doesn't always mean free from trouble!"

Eliot roamed through Mickey's Sports, browsing shelves stocked with tennis rackets and baseball bats. His younger brother, Sean, was searching for a new goalkeeper's jersey in the soccer aisle. Soccer tryouts started on Monday, and Sean wanted a new jersey for good luck.

As Eliot headed back toward the soccer gear, he spotted an athletic boy looming over Sean. "Sean must have bumped into a friend," he thought. Then he saw the kid jab Sean with a finger. "Hey!" Eliot shouted.
Sean's face turned bright red when he saw Eliot rushing toward him.
"Stay off the soccer field, loser!" the kid snarled before he stalked off, snickering.
"Who was that?" Eliot asked.
Sean held up a lime green jersey. "What do you think?" he joked weakly. "Does this go with my red hair and freckles?"
Before Eliot could reply, Sean shoved the jersey back in a pile on the shelf. "Let's get out of here. I can't afford a new jersey anyway."
On Monday Eliot wasn't expecting to see Sean until dinnertime, after his first tryout session had ended. But when Eliot entered the kitchen after school, Sean was perched on a counter stool.
"Sean! What are you doing here?"
"I live here," he said sarcastically. "Remember?"
"That's not what I meant," Eliot said. "Why aren't you at tryouts?"
"Because I'm not trying out."
"What?"
"I won't make the team. So what's the point?"
"The point is, you love soccer," Eliot said. "And you've been preparing for tryouts for months."
"That was before I—" Sean's mouth abruptly snapped shut.

"Before what?" Eliot demanded. Suddenly he flashed back to the scene at Mickey's Sports. "It's that kid from the store! He's the reason you skipped tryouts. You can't let him bully you into staying on the sidelines!"
"It's my own fault," Sean said. "I shouldn't have bragged about my goalie skills to him."
"Whoa." Eliot held up a hand. "It's not your fault. That kid is a bully, plain and simple." He frowned. "Has he harmed you physically?"

Sean shook his head. "George just threatens to hurt me. Plus, he posts mean stuff about me on social media. I figured he'd finally leave me alone if I sat out tryouts this year." He sighed. "I can try out next year."

"No way," Eliot said firmly. "You're not allowing some dumb bully to sabotage your soccer tryout." He glanced at the clock. "I'm driving you back to school. I'll give you some tips for dealing with bullies on the way."

On Friday afternoon Eliot parked at the soccer field. "Today's the day," he thought anxiously. On the field the players huddled around Coach as she announced the names and positions of the players who'd made the team. Eliot didn't see George in the huddle.
A few minutes later, Sean approached the car, head down.
"Uh-oh," Eliot thought.
Then Sean lifted his head—and grinned!
Eliot hopped out of the car. "You made the team!"
"Yep. I'm the starting goalie!" Sean said as Coach joined them.
Coach shook Sean's hand. "Sean, you demonstrated great leadership on Monday by asking me to talk with everyone about bullying. It turns out you weren't the only one having issues with George."
"Talking to an adult," Eliot thought with a smile. "That's a brilliant strategy for dealing with bullies. I wonder who thought of it."
"Teamwork is important, and one bully can hurt the whole team," Coach went on. "I'm sorry I didn't know about the situation sooner. We now have a strict no-bullying policy, thanks to you."
A few minutes later Eliot turned his car onto Main Street.
"Where are we going?" Sean asked
"Back to Mickey's Sports," he said. "To celebrate our victory, I'm going to buy you that green jersey!"
Matt’s family just moved to a new town. He needs to go to a new school. He is also going to need to make new friends. But it’s not easy to make new friends in a new school.
"This is Matt. I’m sure you’ll make him feel welcome." Mrs. Emory introduced him to the class. Matt sat next to a girl named Georgia.
"Hi, I’m Georgia!" she said.
Matt pretended to tie his shoelace. He was too shy to talk to Georgia.
Matt’s first day of school wasn’t too bad. At least no one else tried to talk to him.
"You’re the new kid, right?" asked Jeff after school.
"Do you want to play basketball with us?" asked a boy named Spike. Matt shook his head.
"Okay, see you tomorrow!" said Jeff.
"Okay, see you tomorrow!" said Spike.
Matt was feeling angry with himself. "Why didn’t I say something?" he said aloud. "They probably think I’m stupid!"

Matt wasn’t stupid. He was just very shy. At his old school, it took Matt almost a year to make friends. He never felt comfortable speaking to people. Matt wished he could live on a deserted island. That way he would never have to say anything to anyone.
After school, Matt watched the soccer team practicing. Matt’s new school had a very good soccer team. In fact, they were one of the top teams in the league.
"But Coach, I’ll be better soon!" moaned Ben. Ben was the team’s midfielder. He had broken his leg during the last match.
"Are you new here? I’m Coach Klein," a voice called out.
"Hi, I’m Ben!" the boy with crutches said to Matt.
"Immad," Matt mumbled.
"What?" asked Ben.
"I’m Matt," he said more clearly this time.
"Matt, have you ever played soccer before?" Coach Klein asked.
Matt answered, "Well, sort of."
Matt used to play soccer with his friends from his old neighborhood. But he had never played on a team before. Ben promised to help Matt become a good midfielder.
"I don’t know if I can do it," Matt said in a low voice.
"What? I can’t hear a word you’re saying!" Ben said loudly.
Every day after school, Matt practiced with the team. Matt tried his best to be a good midfielder. He ran to head the ball but collided with Victor.
"You’re supposed to call it!" shouted Victor.
"Matt! When you’re going for the ball, you must let your teammates know!" Coach Klein told him.
"Sorry," mumbled Matt.
The coach was worried about Matt. "I don’t think it’s going to work with Matt," Coach Klein said to Ben. "We need to find someone else."
"Coach Klein, please give Matt another chance. Look at how he moves!" Ben pleaded. "Matt just needs to learn about teamwork. I’ll help him!" Ben said.
"Soccer is about teamwork," Ben explained. "Everyone is like a different instrument in an orchestra. We need to play together in harmony. You have to show that you are part of the team!"
"Luke!" Matt called out and kicked the ball to him.

At Matt’s first match, he was very nervous. Matt tried to concentrate on what Ben had said about teamwork. Matt noticed that Victor needed help. Matt opened his mouth to speak, but no sounds came out. Matt’s team lost one to zero.
"It’s all my fault," Matt thought to himself after the game.
"Hey, you played well today," Victor said as he came up to Matt. "It was your first match. Next time you’ll do better."

Matt’s team was not angry with him for losing the game. "Teamwork! Orchestra! Harmony!" Matt repeated to himself at the next practice. Suddenly he saw the ball flying at Georgia. "Watch out!" he yelled, jumping in front of it.
"Thanks, Matt," Georgia smiled.
Matt decided to do his best and be a true member of the team.
"Matt!" Victor called and passed him the ball.
"Luke! Here!" Matt kicked the ball to Luke. From then on, Matt began to play much better. His team won every game. Matt and his team were going to the championship!
Finally it was the day of the big game.
"Don’t look at the ball!" the coach said before the game. "Don’t look at the goal. Look at your teammates. Remember! You are all champions whether we win or lose!"

After the first half, the teams were tied at one to one. Suddenly Matt saw an opportunity to score near the end of the game. His throat felt dry and his mouth was heavy. But he knew his team was depending on him.
"Luke! Over here!" he shouted loudly. Luke passed the ball, but a player from the other team tackled Matt and knocked him down. Matt’s teammates crowded around him.
"Matt! Are you all right?" Luke bent over him.
"We got a penalty kick! This is our big chance, Matt!" encouraged Victor.

Matt slowly got up. He had to take the penalty kick. Matt never felt so scared in his life. The championship depended on him. He remembered all of the coach’s advice and decided he would try his best for his new friends. He kicked the ball as hard as he could past the goalkeeper. Matt’s kick scored a goal. Matt’s team was the new soccer champion!
"We won! You did it, Matt!" shouted Ben.
"No, we did it! All of us did it together!" Matt said. The coach was right. Everyone was a champion.

Molly and her mother were shopping for clothes on a Saturday afternoon, but every time Molly found something she liked, her mother said, "That’s too expensive, Molly." In the end, Molly’s mother chose an ugly pair of pants.
"I’m never going to wear them!" Molly complained.
Molly’s mother was very careful about spending money.
"Money doesn’t grow on trees," she always said.
"Oh, hi, Molly!" It was Molly’s friend Erica, who was shopping with her mother in the same store.
"Hi, Erica!" Molly said.
"Things are so expensive these days, aren’t they?" said Erica’s mom.
"Yes, I can’t believe the prices!" agreed Molly’s mother.
"Mom, I want that!" said Erica, pointing to an expensive face cleanser.
"Of course, honey. One? Two? No, let’s take three." Erica’s mother put some bottles into her shopping cart. "Well, we should get going. Good-bye!"
"Mom? Can I have some too?" asked Molly.
"Honey, this is really overpriced," Molly’s mother answered, "but if you want, we can get one."
"No, I want more," Molly said.
"One is more than enough," her mother said firmly.
Molly’s family wasn’t poor, but her parents didn’t buy Molly whatever she wanted. "Money isn’t everything," her father would say. "The real valuable things in life cannot be bought with money."
"And money doesn’t grow on trees," her mother would add.
The next day, Molly and her friends were looking at magazines at Jenny’s house. "Wow! I’m going to ask my mom to buy me this!" Esther exclaimed, pointing to the dress in a fashion ad.
"Oh, this is so nice! I’ll tell my dad I want this for my birthday!" Sharon said.
"See what I got?" Jenny held up a pretty blue shirt.
"It’s so cute! How much was it?" asked Sharon.
"I don’t know, but it has a matching hat. See?"

Molly felt so jealous of her friends. "Why are my parents so stingy with money?" she thought to herself. As she was walking home, something on the sidewalk caught her eye. Molly bent down to pick it up. It was a purse. "Someone must have dropped it!" she said, looking for the owner.
There was no one around, so Molly opened the purse. She gasped! The purse was filled with cash!

"Oh no! What should I do?" Molly wondered. "I should take it to the police station, but what if the owner never comes to claim it? Maybe I could take just a little bit of money and then take it to the police station?"

At home, Molly did not tell her parents about the purse and went upstairs to bed. As she thought about keeping the money, a strange feeling stirred inside of her, something she had never felt before. Two voices began to argue in her head.
"Take the money," said Molly the Red.
"No! Turn it in to the police!" said Molly the White.
"No one will know if you take it!" said the Red.
"It’s not yours. You can’t keep it!" said the White.
Molly wasn’t sure which voice to listen to, but when she thought of all the things she could buy, she decided to take the money.
"Now you can buy anything you want!" said Molly the Red.
"No, Molly! Don’t do it!" Molly the White begged.
Molly felt that strange feeling grow stronger. "Now you can be like your friends!" the Red whispered excitedly. Molly smiled and ignored the strange feeling inside.
At the store, she realized it felt powerful to have so much money. "I’ll take these two, please," she said, handing two pairs of shoes to the sales clerk.
"Here you go," smiled the clerk. "Thank you and come again!"
Molly also bought a new shirt and jeans, and decided to wear them on her way home. As she left the store, she bumped into her friends.
"Molly! You look so stylish!" admired Erica.
"Are those new jeans?" asked Jenny.
"I love that shirt!" exclaimed Sharon.
"Where did you get the money to buy these things?" Jenny asked.
"I . . . my mom . . . gave . . . money . . ." Molly stammered. "It’s none of your business!" she burst out.

After she spent the rest of the day buying whatever she wanted, Molly took her purchases up to her bedroom. That strange feeling nudged at her heart again. "What is this I’m feeling?" she wondered. It was really bothering her. "I bought everything I wanted, so why am I not happy?"

Molly picked up the empty purse and opened it up again. Inside was a letter. "Dear Mommy," the letter began, "I wish Daddy would recover soon. I don’t have a lot, but here is some money I saved from working. Please use it for Daddy’s hospital bills. I just want Daddy to be well again."

As Molly read the letter, her eyes welled up with tears. "What have I done? What have I done?" she cried aloud. Her heart was aching. "What kind of person am I? I’m a thief!" she moaned. "I hate myself! I hate myself!"
"Molly! Molly! Wake up, honey!" Molly’s mother gently shook her. Molly was in her room, but the shopping bags and new shoes were gone.
"You were having a nightmare," her mother said.

Molly felt something against her back. It was the purse, and the money was still inside. Molly was relieved. She explained how she had found the purse, and confessed that she had wanted to keep the money. "I’m glad it was just a bad dream," Molly said.
"Me too, honey, and I’m proud of you," her mother said.
"How can you be proud of me? I wanted to keep the money!" Molly said.

"But you didn’t. You know that strange feeling you had?" her mother asked. "That was your conscience. It was telling you to do what was right. In the end, you listened to your conscience, your heart, and that’s what’s most important."
"Mom, I learned that having the things I want doesn’t make me happy," Molly said. "Money can’t buy me happiness."
"You’re a good girl. It’s good deeds that make a good heart," her mother said lovingly.
"I’m going to miss you, Brenda," Leah said on the last day of school.
"I’ll call you when I get back from New York," Brenda promised.
"Where is your family going for summer vacation, Leah?" asked Kylie.
"I don’t know yet," Leah admitted. "But I hope it's somewhere awesome."
That evening Leah asked her mother about their family's vacation plans.
"Actually your dad and I were going to discuss that with you and Paul tonight," Mom said.
"Is it a surprise?" Leah asked excitedly.
"Yes," Mom answered mysteriously. "It's somewhere both new and familiar."
"Hmm," Leah thought curiously. "Where could it be?"
Leah was definitely looking forward to her family's trip this year. A year earlier an unexpected hardship had occurred.
"My company decided to lay off workers," Leah’s dad had told them one night at dinner.
"What does 'lay off' mean?" Leah asked.
"It means they are cutting jobs, including mine," he informed her sadly. "I'll find another job, but it might take some time."

Months had passed before Dad found another job. He was relieved to be working again, but his new salary was much lower than his old salary. That meant everyone in the family still had to make sacrifices.
Leah had to give up taking art classes. "When our finances improve, you can resume your art lessons," Dad promised.
That night the family sat down together. "We've been considering where to go this year," Dad began.
"We want to go somewhere to relax and enjoy time together as a family," added Mom. "And finally we thought of the best place to do that."
"Where is it?" Leah blurted out.
Her parents exchanged glances. "At home!" they said in unison.
Paul and Leah were stunned. "Are you kidding?" Paul asked.
Mom and Dad shook their heads. "We're perfectly serious," said Mom.
"We’re not going to Disneyland? Or Vancouver?" Leah asked in dismay.
"You don't have to travel to an exotic destination to enjoy a vacation," Mom said cheerfully.
"But all my friends are traveling somewhere!" Leah choked back her tears. "Brenda is going to New York!"
Her parents seemed unconcerned.
"Our vacation is for three days." Dad opened a notebook. "And during our vacation, there are some essential rules. Rule number one: No television, Internet, or telephone."
"What?" shouted Paul.
"Rule number two," Dad said. "Each of us takes a turn preparing a meal."
"But that's Mom's job," Leah protested.
"I want a vacation too," Mom stated. "And rule number three: We spend most of our time together. We are not to isolate ourselves."
"Ugh." Leah groaned. This was going to be the strangest—and worst—family vacation ever.
On the first day of vacation, Leah and Paul were in the family room. Leah had found some books to read.
Paul was looking for something. "Where’s the remote?" he called.
"Rule number one, Paul," Dad reminded him. "No television." He held up a box. "How about working on this with me?"
"What is it?" asked Paul.
"A model airplane," said Dad.
Paul shrugged. "Sure."
Mom sat down next to Leah. "Can I keep you company?"
"Okay." Leah looked up from her book as her mother started working on something at the table. "What's that, Mom?"
"A jigsaw puzzle. And I could definitely use your help." Mom moved over to make room for Leah, and the two of them worked on the puzzle for a while.
That night Dad prepared dinner.
"I hope he doesn’t burn the kitchen down!" whispered Mom to Leah and Paul.
"I hope whatever he makes is edible!" Leah said with a giggle.
"Hey! No insulting the chef!" Dad shouted from the kitchen.
Everyone sat down and looked at the food.
"Just try it. You’re going to love it!" Dad said.
Leah wasn't sure what it was, but she sampled the meal anyway. "Actually this is pretty good, Dad."
After dinner the family looked at some old photos. Soon everyone was trading memories about when Leah and Paul were younger.
"Oh, I remember this picture," said Mom. "That was Paul’s first bicycle."
"Hey, I remember that bike. What happened to it?" Paul asked.
The next morning Leah saw that Paul was up early.
"I'm reporting for chef duty," Paul said.
"What are you making for breakfast, Paul?" Mom wanted to know.
"The only thing I know how to make," said Paul.
"Hot dogs? For breakfast?" Leah burst out. "That sounds absolutely delicious!"
Later that day Leah and Paul listened to some music together. And before bedtime, the family played a board game together. It was Leah and Dad versus Paul and Mom.
Soon Leah landed on the history category.
"Name the young Macedonian leader who conquered Persia at the age of 25," Paul read aloud. "You can’t help her, Dad!"
"I got it!" Leah called triumphantly. "Alexander the Great!"
"Wow, how did you get to be so intelligent?" Dad asked.
On the last day of the vacation, everyone did whatever he or she wanted. Leah read a book. Mom painted her toenails. Dad and Paul worked on the airplane model together.
"Ta-da!" They proudly displayed the airplane when it was finally finished.
"It looks fantastic," said Leah.
"Dad and I make a good team," Paul said proudly.
"This was one of the most relaxing vacations I ever had," Dad announced later on.
"I agree." Mom nodded. "I got to spend a lot of quality time with my children and my husband."
"I got to build a model airplane!" Paul said, grinning at Dad.

Leah sat, quietly contemplating the vacation for a minute. Last week she had not been looking forward to her family's vacation at all. While her friends were traveling to faraway destinations, she'd be stuck here, with only boring stuff to do. But she had realized something.
Leah smiled at Mom, Dad, and Paul. "Spending time with your family—even when you stay at home—is the best vacation ever!"
Jin wanted to have a party. "Mom, can I have a slumber party?" she asked her mother one evening.
"A slumber party? You mean invite some friends to sleep over at our house?" Mother said.
"Yes. May I? Please?" Jin pleaded with her mom.
The next day at school, Jin invited three of her friends to her slumber party.
"When is it?" Rachel asked.
"This Saturday. Come around four o’clock," Jin said.
"What should we bring?" Mandy asked.
"Your toothbrush and pajamas."
On the day of the slumber party, Jin was busy cleaning her room when her brother Min opened the door. "How many girls are coming?" he asked.
"None of your business! Go away!" Min was a troublemaker, but Jin was not worried. No one would ruin her party─not even her brother!
At four o’clock, Rachel, Mandy, and Fran arrived at Jin’s house. "We’re going to have so much fun!" The girls giggled excitedly.
"What should we do first?" Fran asked.
"Let’s make cookies!" Mandy suggested. The girls made chocolate chip cookies. When they were ready, Min rushed into the kitchen.
"Cookies! My favorite!" he yelled and grabbed some cookies.
"Get out! Those are our cookies!" Jin shouted.
Min took some more cookies and ran out of the kitchen.
Jin had rented some videos to watch with her friends. The girls took their cookies to the living room and sat down to watch. The first movie was really exciting.
"Oh, what’s going to happen next?" Mandy said, covering her mouth.
"Shh! This is the most important part . . ." Fran’s eyes got big. Suddenly the channel switched to a soccer game.
"What happened?" the girls cried out. Jin looked around. There, behind the couch, was Min holding the remote control.
"Min!" Jin shouted loudly. She went and told her parents everything Min had done.
"Min, you promised not to bother your sister and her friends," Father reminded him sternly.
"Don’t even go near Jin’s room! Do you understand?" Mother said.
"Stay away from us!" Jin yelled at him. She took some pizza from the kitchen, and the girls all went up to her room to eat it. After they ate the pizza, the four friends decided to have some fun.
"Let me do your hair!" Rachel said.
But Mandy had an even better idea. "Look what I brought!"
"Makeup!" screamed the girls.
"It’s my sister’s. I borrowed it for tonight!" Mandy giggled. In no time at all, all the girls had fancy hairstyles and glamorous makeup.
"You look great!" Fran admired Rachel’s eyes.
"You look like Britney Spears!" Jin said to Mandy.

Suddenly the girls all stopped and looked at each other. "Let’s make a band!" they shouted. The girls danced and sang their favorite songs. They were having so much fun that it was past ten o’clock before they knew it. The friends changed into their pajamas, and Jin’s parents came up to say good night.
"Don’t stay up too late, girls," Jin’s father said.
"If you get hungry, there’s some cake in the kitchen," Mother said.
"Thank you. Good night!" the girls called out.
After Jin’s parents closed the door to the room, Fran turned to the others. "Well, good night, girls!" Fran said.
Rachel, Mandy, and Jin stared at her. "Fran! We’re going to stay up all night!" Mandy said.
"But we already did everything," Fran complained.
"We still haven’t done the most exciting part of a slumber party." Rachel smiled.
"Ghost stories!" everyone screamed.
Jin went first. She told them a scary story about a woman who was murdered by her husband. "People say they can still see her ghost searching for her husband."

"Now it’s my turn," Rachel said. Rachel’s story was even scarier than Jin’s. It was about a strange man who only killed girls. "The little girl thought she was safe, but she suddenly heard footsteps. No one ever saw that girl again."
"What . . . what did he look like?" Mandy whispered.
"They say he wore a long cloak and had spiky hair." Rachel pulled her hair up.
"That was so scary!" Fran shivered.
"Let’s take a break and have some cake," Jin suggested. They all went down to the kitchen in the dark. "Don’t turn the lights on," Jin whispered.
"Ouch! I can’t see anything," complained Mandy.
"Shh! You’ll wake everyone up!" Rachel covered Mandy’s mouth.
"I got the cake," Jin said quietly after they reached the kitchen. The girls tiptoed quietly back toward Jin’s room.
"What was that?" whispered Rachel.
"It’s not me!" Mandy said.
They saw a strange shadow approaching. "Oh . . . oh . . . l-look!" Fran pointed.
"It’s him! He’s here!" Rachel’s voice quivered.
The girls screamed as loud as they could, and Jin threw the cake in the air. When they heard the noise, Jin’s parents came running.
"What’s going on here?" shouted Jin’s father.
The four friends were crying and holding onto each other. "He’s here! He’s going to kill us!" cried Fran.
"There’s nobody here," Jin’s mother said.
The girls stopped crying and opened their eyes. "But we all saw him," Mandy wiped some cream from the cake away from her eyes. The friends looked puzzled.
Suddenly there was a sound from behind the door. It was Min.
"Is this who you saw?" smiled Jin’s mother.
"Min!" screamed the girls.
"This time it wasn’t your brother’s fault," Father said. Min had woken up and was thirsty. He had gone to the kitchen to get a glass of water.
"I hope you learned a lesson," Mother said. The girls giggled and soon everyone was laughing.
"Thank you for everything," Jin said to her parents the next evening.
"Did everyone have a good time?" asked Mother.
"Oh yes! It was the best slumber party ever!" Jin smiled at everyone.
"Good. Next week we’re having another one!" Mother said. "This time it’s Min’s turn."

Amy looked in the mirror. She needed a haircut. Her bangs covered her eyes. Amy was going to meet her friends in one hour. They were going to watch a movie. The more Amy looked at her hair, the more she wanted to cut it.
Then Amy got an idea. "I know what I'll do," Amy said aloud. "I'll cut it myself. After all how hard can it be?"
First, Amy took some scissors out of the drawer. Next, she wet her hair. Then, Amy combed her bangs straight. She began to cut. Snip. Snip. Snip.
Amy opened her right eye. It was looking good so far. Amy continued to cut the rest of her bangs. Snip. Snip. Snip.

Amy stood back and looked at herself. She noticed a few strands weren't even. So she placed her left hand on her forehead and pushed the hair down. Snip. Snip. Snip. Amy let go of her left hand. Her bangs sprang up.

"Argh!" Amy screamed. Amy's bangs were much higher than her eyebrows now. She looked quite ridiculous. Amy looked at her watch. She still had time to fix her hair. Amy squeezed some hair gel onto her hands. Then she put it on her hair.
"Argh!" Amy screamed. Now her hair looked like it had been struck by lightning.
Amy was running out of time. "Oh! Why did I cut my own hair!" she moaned.
Amy ran to her room. She pulled out a colorful scarf and wrapped it around her head. Now she looked like a fortune-teller.
Amy pulled out a box from her closet. She took out a hat with a large feather.
Now she looked like her grandmother. Amy pulled out another hat. She put it on and ran out of the house.
"Hi, Amy! Why are you wearing that hat?" asked Lisa.
"Oh, I . . . I felt cold . . . " lied Amy.
"Then why are you wearing shorts?" asked Sherry.
"Hey, the movie's going to start!" said Amy.
"If you're hot, Amy, you should take your hat off," whispered Sherry.
"I'm fine!" Amy whispered back.
"Hey, your hat is blocking my view," said a boy. "Would you mind taking it off please?"

Amy didn't want her friends to see her haircut, but she had no choice. She slowly took the hat off. "Whew!" Amy sat back in her seat, relieved. Since the theater was so dark, no one could see her hair.
"Let's go get some ice cream," said Lisa.
"Will you please take that hat off?" asked Sherry.
Amy pulled her hat tighter over her head. "The last one to the ice-cream shop is a rotten egg!" Lisa and Sherry shrugged their shoulders and ran after Amy.
"Hello, girls! Lovely day, isn't it?" called out Mrs. James.
"Hello, Mrs. James! Hello, Oscar!" Oscar was so happy to see the girls. The girls bent down to pet him.

Oscar began to sniff Amy's hat. "No, Oscar, good doggie. Stop it, Oscar!" Amy dropped her ice cream. "Oh, my ice cream!" cried Amy. Oscar pulled the hat right off Amy's head and ran off. Amy put her hands on her head and tried to cover her hair.
"Amy! Your hair!" screamed Lisa and Sherry. Amy slowly lowered her hands. It was too late! Her friends saw her haircut. "What happened?" asked Lisa.

"I wanted to cut my own hair . . . " Amy began. Amy realized how funny she must have looked wearing the winter hat in the middle of summer. Suddenly the three girls burst out laughing. They laughed and laughed.
"Okay, but what am I going to do? My hair looks terrible!" said Amy.
"I have an idea," said Sherry. She took out two pins from her hair. "There. How does that look?"
"Oh, you look cute! I kind of like your haircut!" said Lisa.
Amy looked in a mirror. "Oh, I do look kind of cute!" said Amy. The three girls laughed again.
"Did you have a good time?" asked Mother.
"Yes, we had fun."
"Good. Oh, Amy, I noticed your hair was getting long. I think you need a haircut."
Kevin is a regular boy in the fifth grade at Hillside Elementary School. Like most boys his age, he doesn’t really like doing his homework.
One day his teacher, Ms. Rose, said, "Kevin, can you come up and write question five from the math homework on the board?"
"Um, well, I, um, well, no," Kevin stammered.
"Why not?" said Ms. Rose. "Where is your homework?"
"Well, you see," replied Kevin, "last night, after I finished my math homework, there was a problem."
"Really? What kind of problem, Kevin?" said Ms. Rose with surprise.
Kevin thought quickly and said, "A terrible problem. You see, after my family went to sleep, a fire started in my house and my homework was burned."
"A fire! Oh my, was anyone hurt?" asked Ms. Rose.
"Well, actually, my sister was burned a little. She went to the hospital, but she is okay now," Kevin replied in a brave voice.
A girl named Suzy asked, "Kevin, did your whole house burn down?"
Excitedly, Kevin replied, "Yes, it was a very large fire and the whole house was on fire. There was smoke everywhere, and the flames were reaching into the sky."
"You must have been very scared, Kevin," said Ms. Rose.
"I sure was," he answered. "For a moment I thought that I was going to die."
From the back of the room, Ted asked, "How did you get out of your house, Kevin?"
"I got out of my house by . . . by . . . " Kevin thought for a moment. "A fire fighter came to the window of my room. He pulled me out onto his ladder and carried me to safety."
Ms. Rose started to become suspicious. "You are very lucky," she said. "You could have been killed. By the way Kevin, what time did the fire start?"
"I’m not exactly sure, but I think about 10:30 at night," Kevin replied.
Then Ted shouted, "Hey Kevin, how many fire trucks came to your house to put out the fire?"
"I’d say about five," Kevin replied quickly. "There were two really big ladder trucks and one truck for the water. There were also two smaller trucks."
"It must have been very loud," said Ms. Rose. "Did many people come and watch?"
"Yes, everyone from the neighborhood was there," said Kevin. "It was very loud."
"How did the fire start?" asked Ms. Rose.
"It started in the kitchen. There was a cloth that was too close to the oven, and it caught on fire," said Kevin.
Ms. Rose was about to catch Kevin. "Who was cooking at 10:30 p.m.?" she inquired.
"My mother was cooking," answered Kevin.
"But Kevin, you said that everyone was sleeping when the fire started," questioned Ms. Rose.
"Well, yes, no. I forgot," stammered Kevin.
"And Kevin," said Ms. Rose, "you said it was a loud fire and everyone saw it, but it was not on the news this morning."
"Well, maybe it was too late for the news people," he replied.
"Okay, Kevin," Ms. Rose said, knowing that Kevin was trapped. "I am going to call your mother to ask her if she needs any help from our class. Wait just a moment, and I’ll be right back."
"No!" pleaded Kevin.
"Why not?" she asked.
"Well, you see, my mother is . . ."
"The truth!" demanded Ms. Rose.
"There wasn’t really a fire," Kevin admitted.
"But you told us that your sister was hurt," said Suzy.
"And you told us that you were rescued by a fire fighter," said Ted.
"And you told us that five fire trucks came to your house," replied another boy.
"Kevin is a liar!" shouted all the children.

Ms. Rose looked at Kevin and explained, "Sometimes a small lie can grow into a big lie. You started with one lie. Then, because of your first lie, you needed to tell another lie. Those two lies led to another lie and then another lie. And this big lie means seven days detention for you, young man. So what did you learn today?" asked Ms. Rose.
"I should tell the truth," said Kevin in a soft voice.
"That’s right. The more you lie, the more you need to lie."
Christy’s family was moving. She was very sad. Christy did not want to leave her friends.
"Don’t worry, honey. You’ll make new friends," Mom said.
"You’ll love the new house too," said Dad. But Christy was still sad.
Christy did not like her new school. The kids did not speak to her. They did not play with her. Christy did not have any friends.
"What did you do at school today?" asked Dad.
"I’m sure there are many nice kids in your class," said Mom. Her parents were very worried.
One day after school, Christy was walking home alone. She saw a little park. "I am going to take a walk in that park," Christy said to herself.
The next day Christy was smiling. "Can I play in the park after school?" Christy asked cheerfully.
"With who, Christy?" asked Mom.
"With my new friend," smiled Christy.
"Of course you can," Mom and Dad said happily.
During lunchtime Christy ate only half of her ham sandwich. All day long she was smiling. Christy could not wait for school to be over. She wanted to go to the park to see her new friend.
"Did you have fun in the park?" asked Dad.
"Oh yes," answered Christy.
"What’s your friend’s name?" asked Mom.
"Hammie!" Christy giggled.
On Saturday Christy went to the park to see her new friend. "Do you want some of my sandwich? No one at school wants to be my friend. You’re the only friend I have, Hammie."
Christy was helping her mom make dinner. "Why don’t you invite your friend for dinner?" Mom asked.
"Uh, I think he’s shy," Christy answered quickly.
"Christy, is your friend a boy?" Mother said with surprise.
"Excuse me, I have to get something from my room!"
"What’s going on?" asked Dad.
"Christy’s new friend Hammie is a boy!" Mom said.
"A boy! You mean Christy has a boyfriend?" said Dad. Christy’s parents were worried once again.
One day there was a new girl in Christy’s class. "Class, this is Mina. Her family just moved here," said Mrs. Peters. "Mina, go and sit next to Christy."
"Hi, Christy! Can I sit here?" asked Mina.
"Sure," said Christy. The two girls began talking.
"Let’s walk home together!" said Mina.
"Well, I have to meet my friend," said Christy. "Do you want to meet my friend?"
The two girls chatted all the way to the park.
It was already dark outside. Christy was not home yet. Her mom and dad were very worried. They knew she was at the park with Hammie.
"Do you know what time it is, young lady?" Dad said angrily.
"I’m sorry. I was in the park . . . " began Christy.
"We know Hammie is your boyfriend!" shouted Mom and Dad together. "Go to your room! You are in big trouble!"
Christy’s parents were very upset. They did not know what to do. Then the phone rang.
"My name is Mina. I’m Christy’s friend."
"I’m sorry, Mina, but Christy can’t come to the phone right now," said Mom.
"Can you tell Christy that I am going to bring some extra sandwiches for Hammie tomorrow?" Mina said.
"You know Hammie? Tell me all about him. What does he look like? How old is he?" Christy’s mom was getting upset again.
"Hammie is a raccoon," said Mina.
"Christy, we’re so sorry for shouting at you." Mom hugged Christy.
"We didn’t know Hammie was a raccoon," said Dad.
"We thought he was your secret boyfriend," said Mom.
"I was so lonely until I met Hammie in the park," said Christy. "Every day he came to play with me. He was my only friend."

The next day Christy went with Mina and her parents to the park. Soon Hammie came to say hello to his friends. "Mom, Dad, this is Hammie, my old friend," Christy said. "And this is Mina, my new friend."

Bobby loves to read books. He reads every chance he gets. He reads fiction and nonfiction. He reads history and biography. Bobby also loves mystery and science fiction. But Bobby's favorite books are about science, especially plants.
All of the kids in school call Bobby bookworm. But they don't always mean it in a nice way.
A lot of kids tease Bobby and call him bad names. But Bobby tries to ignore them.
One day Bobby's class went on a field trip to Rockbridge Park. Bobby was in a group with five other students. One of them, named Kyle, made fun of Bobby all the time.
"Where's your book, bookworm?" Kyle said.
"Class, stay in your groups, please!" Mrs. Murphy called.
The class followed Mrs. Murphy and the park ranger as they walked into the forest. The ranger explained about the different types of trees and plants.
Suddenly Bobby felt someone grab his bag.
"Hey, bookworm! What's this?" teased Kyle.
"Give me back my book!" said Bobby.
"Come and get it!" said the boys.
Bobby wanted his book, so he ran after Kyle and Frank. Kyle and Frank ran deeper and deeper into the woods. Bobby finally caught up with them.
"Give me back my book!" demanded Bobby.
"My pleasure!" said Kyle. He threw the book on the ground.
"Let's get out of here," said Frank.
"Which way do we go?" asked Kyle.
"Uh, Kyle, I think we're lost," said Frank.
"I'm getting cold," said Kyle.
"I'm hungry," Frank whined.
"Me too. And my feet are killing me," complained Kyle.
Bobby quietly took out some candy. He gave it to Frank and Kyle.
"Hey, thanks, bookworm," said the boys.
"Hey, look! Let's eat those berries!" said Kyle.
"No! Don't eat those! They're poisonous!" shouted Bobby. "That's the red baneberry. The flower petals are white and it smells like a rose. But the berries and roots are poisonous," said Bobby.
The three boys walked and walked. They looked for the rest of the class.
"I'm getting tired," cried Frank.
"Let's sit here and rest," said Kyle.
"Wait! Don't sit there!" shouted Bobby. "That's poison ivy!"
"Gosh, how do you know so much about plants?" asked Frank.
"I read about them in books," answered Bobby. "Come on, I'll show you some other poisonous plants and berries."

Bobby led the two boys along the path. They stopped in front of bushes and trees. Bobby explained about the different flowers and plants. The boys were very interested in what they saw. Soon they forgot they were lost!
"Wow! You're so smart," said Kyle.
"I wish I knew as much as you do," said Frank.
"It's not because I'm smarter than you," said Bobby. "It's because I read about plants in books."
Suddenly they heard a familiar voice. "Kyle! Frank! Bobby!" It was Mrs. Murphy. She was with the park ranger.
"Are you okay?" asked Mrs. Murphy.
"We were very worried because the forest has many dangers and poisonous plants!" said the park ranger.
"Bookworm . . . I mean, Bobby is an expert on plants, so we were okay," said Kyle.
"Well, you boys are in big trouble! You will go to the library and do research on all the poisonous plants in North America. Then you will present it to the class," said Mrs. Murphy.
The three boys looked at each other and smiled.
"What are you smiling about?" asked Mrs. Murphy.
"Nothing, Mrs. Murphy. We're sorry!" the boys said together.
From then on, every Saturday, the three friends went to the library. Kyle and Frank soon realized why Bobby loved to read so much. They decided to start a club. They called it The Bookworm Club.
Pluck woke up one morning earlier than usual. He could hear his friends outside singing, "Get up! Get up! It's a new day!"
"What should I do today?" he wondered. "I could pick worms, glide through the air, or clean my feathers. But none of that sounds like fun."
Pluck was not very excited about the new day. So Pluck flew off to the riverbank to visit his friend, Duckie.
"Hi Duckie!" Pluck called as he swooped down to the bank.
"Well hello, Pluck. What a nice surprise to see you!" said Duckie.
"Do you have any exciting plans for today?" said Pluck. "I am bored and don't know what to do."
"Hmm." Duckie had to think hard. "You could fly with me up and down the river, or we could dig in the mud to cool off our feet," he offered.
"No, thanks," said Pluck. "Well, if we have nothing to do at least we can be bored together."
So Pluck and Duckie settled into the bank.
They watched the flowers opening their faces to the sun. The flowers bent their stems to get as close to the light as possible. "Ooh!"

They watched the fish jump at the bugs, trying to catch some lunch. The fish jumped high out of the water and made a lot of ripples when they fell back in. One fish splashed so much that he got Pluck and Duckie wet! "Hey!"
While Pluck and Duckie were trying to shake off the water, they heard a little voice below them start to complain. "Please stop! You are soaking my home!"
They looked at the ground and saw a row of ants marching food into their hole. Sure enough, the water from their wings was getting the ground wet.
"Oops! We're sorry!" Duckie said, and they moved to the side.
"Those ants are really strong!" said Pluck, sounding very impressed. "Their food is five times bigger than they are!"

After the ants left, Pluck and Duckie looked around. There was nothing left to see. Duckie lay down and stared at the sky. "That cloud looks like Big Farmer Parton!" said Duckie, sounding very sure of himself.

"Yeah, I see him! And next to him is Dolly, his little girl!" said Pluck. As they lay there finding shapes in the clouds, the clouds began to turn pink and purple. This made the pictures in the sky even more beautiful and helped their imaginations find new shapes in the clouds.

Eventually the pinkish purple colors began to turn to dark blue. While Pluck and Duckie were watching the clouds, the sun had begun to set. The flowers began to close their petals. The fish stopped jumping. The ants shut the door to their hole for the night. Pluck and Duckie could no longer see the cloud shapes.
Pluck stood up and looked at Duckie. "Oh no! Duckie, we've wasted the whole day! We didn't do anything important!" he said disappointedly.
"We didn't waste the day. We did nothing!" said Duckie.
"What?" asked Pluck, sounding confused.

"We don't have to be busy working to have an important day. Watching everyone else go about their day helped us appreciate the world around us. I had a wonderful time, but I won't be able to do it again for a little while."
"Why not?" asked Pluck. He was starting to like the idea of doing nothing every day.
"Because I have work to do tomorrow. Would you like to help?"
"Sure," Pluck agreed. "Goodnight, Duckie," he said, as he watched him waddle home.
"See you tomorrow for a brand new adventure," Duckie called back.
Pluck flew home for a good night's sleep.
One fine day Skunk was playing with his friends. "Ha! This is a lot of fun!" he said. Then he lifted his tail. "Oops!"
"Ew! What a terrible smell! Skunk made a bad smell. Ha-ha!" said Mouse.
"Yes, ew!" said Rabbit. "Let's go play with someone else. Skunk stinks."
The next day Skunk saw Rabbit and Mouse. Skunk lowered his tail. He did not want to make a bad smell again.
"Hi, Rabbit! Don't you want to play with me?" said Skunk.
"No! Stinky Skunk!" said Rabbit.
"Let's not play with him. He smells bad," said Mouse.
Skunk cried and ran to his cave. "No one wants to play with me." He did not come out until nighttime. He was very sad.
One day Skunk was very thirsty. He left the cave and went to the pond. He still held his tail very low.
"Oh, there is Rabbit," he said. "I must be careful not to make a bad smell."
Rabbit ran past the pond.
"Rabbit, please stop for a moment and play with me," said Skunk. "I will try not to make a bad smell again."
But Rabbit kept running. Skunk felt very sad. He had no friends and no one to play with.
He knew he smelled bad, but there was nothing he could do about it.
Several lonely days passed, and Skunk went for a walk. All of a sudden, Skunk saw that Rabbit was in trouble.
"Oh no! Bear is chasing Rabbit!" said Skunk. "What can I do? Bear is so big and has such big teeth. He might eat me too!"
Skunk decided to run away. Just as Skunk turned around to run, Rabbit saw him. "Skunk, help me! Please!" she cried.
"Oh, poor Rabbit!" thought Skunk. "What should I do? Oh! Maybe my bad smell will chase him away." Skunk went up to Bear. "Let Rabbit go, or I will make a bad smell!" he said.
"Ha-ha!" Bear laughed. "A smell? You are so funny, little Skunk. Let me smell your bad smell."
So Skunk lifted his tail.
"Nooo! Ahhh! Ugh! Ew!" cried Bear, and he ran away.
Rabbit was so happy! She hugged Skunk! "Skunk, your smell saved my life. Hey, everyone! Hooray for Skunk! He saved me from Bear."
"Hooray for Skunk!" the animals cheered.
Skunk became a hero! All the animals surrounded Skunk. "Show us how you scared Bear away," Mouse asked.
"Okay," said Skunk. "I lifted my tail like this . . ."
All the animals held their noses. And then they all laughed.
"Let's go play together," said Rabbit.
"Yes, let's go play!" said Skunk.
On that day, Skunk realized he was perfect just the way he was.
